prompt:
*(Power Question 2002: Power of Association.)* In these problems a *clique* is a non-empty set of students and students may be members of more than one clique. Lowercase letters denote students; uppercase letters denote cliques. For example, $C=abcd$ is a clique of the four students $a,b,c,d$, and $\{abcd,efgh\}$ is a collection of two cliques. $S$ stands for the set of all students (the student body); there is a finite number of students.

At Archimedes Academy (AA) the cliques satisfy the following three conditions.

* **A1.** For any two students, there is exactly one clique of which they are both members.
* **A2.** If a student $a$ is not a member of a clique $C$, then there exists exactly one clique $D$ of which $a$ is a member and that has no members in common with $C$.
* **A3.** There are three students that are not all members of the same clique.

If $S=\{a,b,c,d\}$, determine a collection of cliques that satisfies A1–A3.

solutions.title: All pairs
solutions.body:
Take all six pairs $\{ab,ac,ad,bc,bd,cd\}$.

* A1: any two students form exactly one of these cliques.
* A2: let $C=uv$ be a clique and $x\notin C$; call the fourth student $y$. The cliques containing $x$ are $xu$, $xv$, $xy$, and only $xy$ is disjoint from $uv$. So there is exactly one such clique.
* A3: $a,b,c$ are not all in one clique.

So the collection satisfies A1–A3. ∎

* **A3.** There are three students that are not all members of the same clique.

If $S=\{a,b,c\}$, prove that there is no collection of cliques that satisfies A1–A3.
answer: A3 forces $ab,bc,ca$ to be cliques; then A2 forces singleton cliques, and A2 fails for the clique $c$ and student $a$.

solutions.title: Contradiction with A2
solutions.body:
Suppose such a collection exists. By A3, no clique contains all of $a,b,c$. By A1 the clique through $a,b$ cannot contain $c$, so it is exactly $ab$; likewise $bc$ and $ac$ are cliques.

Apply A2 to the clique $ab$ and the student $c\notin ab$: a clique containing $c$ and disjoint from $ab$ can only be $\{c\}$, so $\{c\}$ must be a clique. Now apply A2 to the clique $\{c\}$ and the student $a\notin\{c\}$: both $\{a\}$ (which is a clique, by the same argument applied to $bc$ and $a$) and $ab$ contain $a$ and are disjoint from $\{c\}$. That is two cliques, contradicting the uniqueness required by A2. ∎

solutions.title: Twelve cliques of three
solutions.body:
Two-student cliques cannot work with nine students (if $ab$, $cd$, $ce$ were cliques, then $c$ would lie in two cliques disjoint from $ab$, violating A2), so try three-student cliques. Take the $12$ cliques
$$\{abc,\ def,\ ghi,\ \ adg,\ beh,\ cfi,\ \ aei,\ hcd,\ fgb,\ \ ahf,\ ecg,\ idb\}.$$
They fall into four groups of three pairwise disjoint cliques, each group partitioning $S$: rows $abc,def,ghi$ and columns $adg,beh,cfi$ of the array $\begin{smallmatrix}a&b&c\\d&e&f\\g&h&i\end{smallmatrix}$, and rows $aei,hcd,fgb$ and columns $ahf,ecg,idb$ of the array $\begin{smallmatrix}a&e&i\\h&c&d\\f&g&b\end{smallmatrix}$.

* A1: the $12$ cliques contain $12\cdot3=36=\binom92$ pairs, and listing them shows that no pair repeats, so each pair of students lies in exactly one clique.
* A2: let $C$ be a clique and $s\notin C$. In the group containing $C$, the three cliques partition $S$, so exactly one clique $D$ in that group contains $s$, and it is disjoint from $C$. Any other clique through $s$ lies in a different group; a clique $K$ meets each of the $9$ cliques outside its group (each of its $3$ students lies in exactly one clique of each group, so in $3$ cliques outside $K$'s group, and these $9$ cliques are distinct by A1); as there are exactly $9$ cliques outside the group, $K$ meets all of them, in particular $C$ when $K$ is in another group. So $D$ is the only one.
* A3: $a,b,d$ are not in a common clique.

∎

solutions.body:
Fix a clique $C$. Every student $s$ lies in some clique of $[C]$: if $s\in C$, take $C$; otherwise by A2 there is a clique through $s$ disjoint from $C$. Two different cliques $E_1,E_2\in[C]$ are disjoint: $E_1$ is exclusive of $C$, and $C$ is exclusive of $E_2$, so by 3 $E_1$ is exclusive of $E_2$. Thus the cliques of $[C]$ partition $S$.

solutions.body:
Take $S=\{a,b,c,d,e,f,g\}$ and the seven cliques $abc,\ ade,\ afg,\ bdf,\ beg,\ cdg,\ cef$.

* H1: the $7$ cliques contain $7\cdot3=21=\binom72$ pairs, and checking the list shows no pair occurs twice, so every pair of students is in exactly one clique.

Cliques in $S_C$ are formed by removing the members of $C$ from the cliques in $S$. Show that $S_C$ satisfies the Archimedean conditions A1–A3:

* **A1.** For any two students, there is exactly one clique of which they are both members.
* **A2.** If a student $a$ is not a member of a clique $C'$, then there exists exactly one clique $D$ of which $a$ is a member and that has no members in common with $C'$.
* **A3.** There are three students that are not all members of the same clique.
answer: The cliques of $S_C$ are the sets $K\setminus C$ with $K\ne C$ a clique of $S$; each $K\setminus C$ has $|K|-1\ge2$ students. Verify A1–A3 from H1–H4.

solutions.title: Verify A1–A3
solutions.body:
The cliques of $S_C$ are the sets $K\setminus C$ for cliques $K
e C$ of $S$. By H2, $|K\cap C|=1$, so $K\setminus C$ has $|K|-1\ge2$ students (H4). Two such sets with two common students come from cliques with two common students, hence from the same clique (H1); so $K\mapsto K\setminus C$ is injective.

By H2, $M$ meets $K$ in exactly one student, which cannot lie in $S_C$, so it lies in $C\cap K=\{t\}$. Thus $M$ contains $s$ and $t$, so $M=L$ by H1.

prompt:
*(Power Question 2002: Power of Association.)* A *clique* is a non-empty set of students (a student may belong to several cliques), and $S$ is the finite set of all students. At Hausdorff High (HH) the cliques satisfy:

* **H1.** For any two students, there is exactly one clique of which both are members.
* **H2.** For any two cliques, there is exactly one student who is a member of both.
* **H3.** There exist three students who are not all members of the same clique.
* **H4.** Every clique has at least three students.

If $|C|=n$ for some clique $C$, find, with proof, the total number of students at Hausdorff High in terms of $n$.

solutions.title: All cliques have size $n$, then use problem 7
solutions.body:
**Step 1: every clique has $n$ students.** Let $K\ne C$ be cliques. They meet in one student. There is a student $s\notin C\cup K$: take $x\in C\setminus K$, $y\in K\setminus C$ (they exist since $|C|,|K|\ge3$ and $|C\cap K|=1$) and let $L$ be the clique through $x,y$; then $L\cap C=\{x\}$, $L\cap K=\{y\}$, and $L$ has a third student (H4) outside $C\cup K$. Now the cliques through $s$ are in bijection with the students of $C$ (each clique through $s$ meets $C$ in exactly one student by H2, and the clique through $s$ and a given $t\in C$ is unique by H1). So the number of cliques through $s$ is $|C|$; by the same argument it is $|K|$. Hence $|K|=|C|=n$.

**Step 2.** By problem 11, $S_C=S\setminus C$ with the cliques $K\setminus C$ satisfies A1–A3, and each of its cliques has $n-1$ students. By problem 7, the number of students of $S_C$ is $(n-1)^2$. Therefore
$$|S|=|C|+|S_C|=n+(n-1)^2=n^2-n+1.$$
(For example $n=3$ gives $7$ students, matching problem 9.)

**Answer: $n^2-n+1$** ∎
